title: Writing Box with Design of Flowering Bush Clover and Sun
medium: Gold, silver togidashimaki-e, hiramaki-e, takamaki-e, cut-out gold foil application

altText: A lacquer box with a gold and silver design of a flowering bush clover plant and a sun, the shining metal standing out against the lacquer ground.

context: A writing box made in Japan in the first half of the 19th century, during the Edo period. It is decorated in lacquer with gold and silver maki-e techniques and cut-out gold foil, with a design of flowering bush clover and the sun. Bush clover is an autumn plant often celebrated in Japanese poetry.

descriptions.k: This fancy box has a plant and a sun on it. The plant has tiny flowers. The picture shines in gold and silver. People used this box to hold writing tools. What would you keep in a box this pretty?
descriptions.g12: This writing box from Japan has a design of bush clover, a plant with small flowers, and a round sun. The pictures are made with gold and silver. Bush clover blooms in autumn. How does the sun make the plant feel? What season do you think it is?
descriptions.g35: This writing box from Japan was made to hold an inkstone, ink stick, and brushes. Its lid shows flowering bush clover and the sun, made with gold and silver in different lacquer techniques. Some parts are raised and some are flat and polished. Bush clover is an autumn plant. Why might a designer choose a plant and a sun for a writing box?
descriptions.g68: This 19th century writing box uses several lacquer techniques at once: togidashi maki-e, in which gold or silver powder is polished until it is level with the surface, hiramaki-e, in which the design is slightly raised, takamaki-e, in which it is built up higher, and cut gold foil. Together they give the design different textures and shine. Bush clover signals autumn. How does the sun change the meaning of the plant, and what might it add to the mood?
descriptions.g910: The box shows how lacquer artists could vary surface within a single design. Different maki-e methods produce flat, slightly raised, and heavily raised effects, while cut gold foil adds crisp accents. Bush clover is a classic autumn motif in Japanese poetry, and pairing it with the sun creates a simple, striking composition. Consider how the maker uses contrast of shine and depth, rather than color, to give the plant life and the sun presence.
descriptions.g1112: This box demonstrates the technical range of Edo-period lacquer: polished togidashi, raised hiramaki-e and takamaki-e, and cut gold foil, all in one design. Bush clover is strongly associated with autumn in poetry, and the sun's inclusion creates a spare composition with possible seasonal or symbolic resonance, though specific intent is not documented in the record. The object also reminds us that function mattered: it housed writing tools. How do technique, motif, and use together shape meaning?

teacherNote.context: A writing box in lacquer with gold and silver maki-e and cut gold foil, first half of the 19th century, Edo period. The design of bush clover and the sun suggests autumn.
directions: Ask students to design a lid with one plant and one celestial object, using only metallic-looking colors.
Compare how this box and the deer box in the archive show autumn.
Discuss how an object's texture can be part of its design even when you cannot touch it.
